subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Attention Economy
description: A quick, practical guide to The Attention Economy.

hook.text: Herbert Simon warned in 1971 that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention.

buildup.text: Tech companies learned this. Every app, notification, and feed competes for your limited attention.

discovery.text: The business model is simple: capture attention, sell it to advertisers. You are the product.

twist.text: Infinite scroll, autoplay, and variable rewards are designed by people who study attention science.

climax.text: Former tech insiders now warn that these tools exploit the same brain circuits as slot machines.

punchline.text: In the attention economy, distraction is the product.

quiz.question: Who warned that information wealth creates attention poverty?

details.summary: In a world of infinite information, attention has become the scarce resource that companies compete for. The attention economy describes how tech platforms, media, and advertisers design products to capture and hold human attention, often at the cost of user wellbeing and autonomy.
details.whyItMatters: The attention economy shapes modern life. Understanding it reveals why apps are addictive, why news is sensationalized, and why protecting your attention is an act of self-defense.
takeaways: Human attention is the scarce commodity in the information age
Tech platforms are designed to maximize attention capture
The concept was articulated by Herbert Simon in 1971

faq.question: Who coined the term attention economy?
faq.answer: Herbert Simon articulated the core idea in 1971, noting that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. Michael Goldhaber developed it further in the late 1990s as the internet made information essentially free and attention became the binding constraint.

faq.question: How do tech companies exploit the attention economy?
faq.answer: They use variable reward schedules, infinite scroll, autoplay, push notifications, and social validation signals like likes to trigger dopamine-driven engagement loops. These design patterns exploit the same brain systems that evolved for survival-relevant alerting.
